concepts.title: Underfitting
concepts.one_liner: Underfitting occurs when a learner fails to optimize the objective on the training data.
concepts.content: A learner may perform poorly for one of two reasons: either it failed to optimize the objective on the training data, or it succeeded on the training data but in a way that does not generalize to the test setting. The former is called underfitting and the latter is called overfitting.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding underfitting helps diagnose why a model performs poorly. It distinguishes between a model that is too simple to capture the data's structure (underfitting) and one that captures noise instead of the signal (overfitting).
concepts.recap_md: - Underfitting is the failure to achieve a low error on the training dataset.

concepts.title: Polynomial Regression
concepts.one_liner: Polynomial regression extends linear regression by using polynomial functions as the hypothesis space.
concepts.content: Polynomial regression is just like linear regression except that the hypothesis space is polynomial functions rather than linear functions, that is, $$\begin{aligned} y = f_{\theta}(x) = \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k \end{aligned}$$ where $K$, the degree of the polynomial, is a hyperparameter of the hypothesis space. We use the least-squares ($L_2$) loss function. Polynomial regression is highly related to linear regression; we can transform a polynomial regression problem into a linear regression problem by rewriting the polynomial as: $$\begin{aligned} \sum_{k=0}^K \theta_k x^k = \theta^\mathsf{T}\phi(x)\\ \quad\quad\quad\quad \phi(x) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ x \\ x^2 \\ \vdots \\ x^K \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}$$ Now the form of $f_{\theta}$ is $f_{\theta}(x) = \theta^\mathsf{T}\phi(x)$, which is a linear function in the parameters $\theta$. Therefore, if we featurize $x$, representing each datapoint $x$ with a feature vector $\phi(x)$, then we have arrived at a linear regression problem in this feature space. The learning problem and closed form optimizer for $L_2$ polynomial regression use a data matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}$: $$\mathbf{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & x^{(1)} & x^{(1)^2} & ... & x^{(1)^K} \\ 1 & x^{(2)} & x^{(2)^2} & ... & x^{(2)^K} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & x^{(N)} & x^{(N)^2} & ... & x^{(N)^K} \\ \end{bmatrix}$$ The matrix $\mathbf{\Phi}$ is an array of the features (columns) for each datapoint (rows). It plays the same role as the data matrix $\mathbf{X}$ in standard linear regression.
concepts.motivation_md: Polynomial regression allows models to capture non-linear relationships between variables while still utilizing the efficient, well-understood optimization tools of linear regression through feature transformation.
concepts.recap_md: - Hypothesis space consists of polynomial functions of degree $K$.

concepts.title: Data Generating Process
concepts.one_liner: The data generating process is the full mechanism, including the true relationship and noise, that produces observed data.
concepts.content: The observed data $\{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ is sampled from a ground truth relationship plus observation noise. We refer to the full process that generates the data as the **data generating process**: $$\begin{aligned} Y &= X^2 + 1 &\triangleleft \quad\text{true underlying relationship}\\ \epsilon &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,1) &\triangleleft \quad\text{observation noise}\\ Y^\prime &= Y + \epsilon &\triangleleft \quad\text{noisy observations}\\ x,y &\sim p(X,Y^{\prime}) &\triangleleft \quad\text{data-generating process} \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between the true underlying signal and the noise in the data generating process is fundamental to building models that generalize to new, unseen data.
concepts.recap_md: - Combines a true underlying relationship with stochastic observation noise.

concepts.title: Approximation Error
concepts.one_liner: Approximation error is the total cost incurred by a model on the training data set.
concepts.content: **Approximation error** is the gap between the model's fit and the training data points. Let $\{x_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}, y_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ be our training data set. Then the approximation error $J_{\texttt{approx}}$ is defined as the total cost incurred on this training data: $$\begin{aligned} J_{\texttt{approx}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}), y_{(\texttt{train})}^{(i)}) \end{aligned}$$ Notice that approximation error is the cost function we minimize in empirical risk minimization.
concepts.motivation_md: Approximation error measures how well a model can 'memorize' or fit the specific data points it was trained on, serving as the primary objective during the training phase.
concepts.recap_md: - Represents the average loss calculated over the training dataset.

concepts.title: Generalization Error
concepts.one_liner: Generalization error is the expected cost incurred when applying a model to new test points from the data generating process.
concepts.content: **Generalization error** is the gap between the model's fit and the ground truth relationship, that is, the expected cost we would incur if we sampled a new test point at random from the true data generating process. Generalization error is often approximated by measuring performance on a heldout validation set, $\{x_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}, y_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, which can simply be a subset of the data that we don't use for training or testing: $$\begin{aligned} J_{\texttt{gen}} &= \mathbb{E}_{x,y \sim p_{\texttt{data}}} [ \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x), y)]\\ &\approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}), y_{(\texttt{val})}^{(i)}) \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: The ultimate goal of machine learning is to perform well on unseen data, making generalization error the most important metric for assessing a model's real-world utility.
concepts.recap_md: - Measures the expected loss over the entire data distribution.

concepts.title: Regularization
concepts.one_liner: Regularization refers to mechanisms that penalize function complexity to avoid overfitting.
concepts.content: **Regularization** refers to mechanisms that penalize function complexity so that we avoid learning too flexible a function that overfits. Typically, regularizers are terms we add to the objective that prefer simple functions in the hypothesis space, all else being equal. They therefore embody the principle of **Occam's razor**. The general form of a regularized objective is: $$\begin{aligned} J(\theta) = \overbrace{\frac{1}{N} \sum^N_{i=1} \mathcal{L}(f_{\theta}(x)^{(i)}, y^{(i)})}^\text{data fit loss} + \underbrace{\lambda R(\theta)}_\text{regularizer} \end{aligned}$$ where $\lambda$ is a hyperparameter that controls the strength of the regularization.
concepts.motivation_md: Regularization helps find a 'Goldilocks' model that is expressive enough to fit the data but simple enough to generalize well to new observations.
concepts.recap_md: - Adds a penalty term $R(\theta)$ to the loss function to discourage complexity.

motivation.text: We should prefer hypotheses (functions f) that are sufficiently expressive to fit the data, but not so flexible that they can overfit the data.

concepts.title: Occam's Razor
concepts.one_liner: Occam's razor is the principle that when multiple functions explain the data, preference should be given to the simplest.
concepts.content: Regularization embodies the principle of **Occam's razor**. When multiple functions can explain the data, give preference to the simplest. In practice, this means penalizing function complexity to avoid learning too flexible a function that overfits, preferring simple functions in the hypothesis space all else being equal.
concepts.motivation_md: This philosophical principle provides a heuristic for model selection: simpler models are less likely to capture random noise and more likely to capture the underlying phenomenon.
concepts.recap_md: - Suggests that the simplest explanation for a set of observations is usually the best.

concepts.title: Lp Regularizer
concepts.one_liner: An Lp regularizer penalizes the Lp norm of the model parameters to encourage simpler functions.
concepts.content: One of the most common regularizers is to penalize the $L_p$ norm of the parameters of our model, $\theta$: $$ R(\theta) = \left\lVert\theta\right\rVert_{p}. $$ The $L_p$-norm of $\mathbf{x}$ is $(\sum_i |x_i|^{p})^{\frac{1}{p}}$. An especially common choice is $p=2$, in which case the regularizer is also known as **Tikonov regression** (or weight decay in neural networks). When $p=1$, the regularizer applied to regression is called the Lasso. For any $p$, the effect is to encourage most parameters to be zero, or near zero. When most parameters are zero, the function takes on a simpler, degenerate form. For example, in a quadratic hypothesis space $\theta_1 x + \theta_2 x^2$, a strong $L_p$ regularizer might force $\theta_2$ to zero if a linear fit is sufficient, embodying Occam's razor by preferring the simpler linear function.
concepts.motivation_md: Lp regularization provides a mathematical way to enforce simplicity by shrinking parameter values, effectively performing feature selection or reducing model sensitivity.
concepts.recap_md: - Penalizes the magnitude of parameters using the $L_p$ norm.

concepts.title: Regularizers as Probabilistic Priors
concepts.one_liner: Regularizers can be interpreted as probabilistic priors that prefer certain solutions over others before looking at the data.
concepts.content: Regularizers can be interpreted as priors that prefer, a priori (before looking at the data), some solutions over others. Under this interpretation, the data fit loss (e.g., $L_2$ loss) is a likelihood function $p(\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1} \bigm | \{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}, \theta)$ and the regularizer is a prior $p(\theta)$. Bayes' rule then states that the posterior $p(\theta \bigm | \{x^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1})$ is proportional to the product of the prior and the likelihood. The log posterior is then the sum of the log likelihood and the log prior, plus a constant. Hence we arrive at the form of a regularized objective.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept provides a formal probabilistic foundation for regularization. By viewing regularizers as priors, we can use Bayesian inference to justify why we penalize certain model parameters and how to balance our pre-existing beliefs with observed data.
concepts.recap_md: - Regularizers act as a prior $p(\theta)$ that encodes preferences for specific types of solutions.

concepts.title: Bayesian Occam's Razor
concepts.one_liner: The Bayesian Occam's razor suggests that simpler hypotheses are more likely because complex hypothesis spaces must spread their prior probability mass more thinly.
concepts.content: The notion of the Bayesian Occam's razor derives priors by noting that more complex hypothesis spaces must cover more possible hypotheses, and therefore must assign less prior mass to any single hypothesis. This follows from the requirement that the prior probability of all possible hypotheses in the hypothesis space must sum to 1. This is why, probabilistically, simpler hypotheses are more likely to be true.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a mathematical justification for the principle of parsimony, explaining why we should prefer simpler models unless the data strongly suggests otherwise.
concepts.recap_md: - Complex hypothesis spaces assign less prior mass to individual hypotheses because the total probability must sum to 1.

concepts.title: Model Capacity and Generalization
concepts.one_liner: Model capacity refers to the expressivity of a hypothesis space, for which the number of parameters is only a rough proxy.
concepts.content: The number of parameters in a model is a rough proxy for model capacity (i.e., the expressivity of the hypothesis space), but it is not the full story. A single parameter with infinite numerical precision can parameterize an arbitrarily complex function and overfit data. Conversely, a model with a million parameters that are heavily regularized (e.g., forced to be zero) may define a simple class of functions that does not overfit. Recent empirical findings show that complex hypothesis spaces like deep nets often do not overfit despite having many more parameters than datapoints.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding that capacity is not just about parameter count helps explain why massive models like deep neural networks can generalize well when properly regularized.
concepts.recap_md: - Model capacity measures the expressivity of a hypothesis space.

motivation.text: A recent empirical finding is that some seemingly complex hypothesis spaces, such as deep nets (which we will see in later chapters), tend not to overfit, even though they have many more free parameters than the number of datapoints they are fit to.

concepts.title: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses as Search Tools

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: Learning can be viewed as a search for truth using three primary tools: data, priors, and hypotheses.
concepts.content:
Learning is akin to searching for a "needle in a haystack," where the needle is the true function and the haystack is the hypothesis space. Three tools help pinpoint this truth:

1. **Data**: Observations of the world (e.g., photos) that prefer mappings fitting the observed evidence.
2. **Priors**: Regularizers that prefer some solutions over others a priori.
3. **Hypotheses**: The set of functions under consideration ($\mathcal{F}$), which places a hard constraint on what can be found.

(see figure: A cartoon of the tools for honing in on the truth.)

In this framework, the hypothesis space $\mathcal{F}$ (white circle) acts as a hard constraint, while the prior (yellow ellipse) and data (green ellipse) act as soft constraints. A learning algorithm searches over $\mathcal{F}$ to maximize the likelihood times the prior, finding a solution in the region where these constraints overlap. While approximation error is low in the data-fitting region, we bias our selection toward the prior's region to improve generalization.
concepts.motivation_md: This framework helps students visualize how different components of machine learning (architecture, regularization, and dataset) interact to isolate a single model from an infinite space of possibilities.
concepts.recap_md: - The hypothesis space provides a hard constraint on possible solutions.

key_passage.text: We have several tools at our disposal to help us pinpoint the location of the needle, and in this section we will focus on the following three: data, priors, and hypotheses. Together these three tools allow us to pinpoint one (or a few) good solutions in the space of all possibilities.

question.text: "Why are you looking there," a cop asks.

motivation.text: In vision, the data is observations of the world like photos and videos. Finding explanations consistent with the observed data is the centerpiece of learning-based vision. The hypothesis space constrains which solutions we can possibly find. If the true solution is not in our hypothesis space, then no amount of data or priors can help us find it.

Learning is akin to searching for a "needle in a haystack," where the needle is the true function and the haystack is the hypothesis space. Three tools help pinpoint this truth:

1. **Data**: Observations of the world (e.g., photos) that prefer mappings fitting the observed evidence.
2. **Priors**: Regularizers that prefer some solutions over others a priori.
3. **Hypotheses**: The set of functions under consideration ($\mathcal{F}$), which places a hard constraint on what can be found.

(see figure: A cartoon of the tools for honing in on the truth.)

In this framework, the hypothesis space $\mathcal{F}$ (white circle) acts as a hard constraint, while the prior (yellow ellipse) and data (green ellipse) act as soft constraints. A learning algorithm searches over $\mathcal{F}$ to maximize the likelihood times the prior, finding a solution in the region where these constraints overlap. While approximation error is low in the data-fitting region, we bias our selection toward the prior's region to improve generalization.

concepts.title: The Trade-off Between Data and Modeling Tools

position.section_title: Three Tools in the Search for Truth: Data, Priors, and Hypotheses

concepts.one_liner: There is a fundamental trade-off where more data reduces the need for strong priors and structural constraints.
concepts.content: A central principle in learning is that the more data you have, the less you need other modeling tools. With enough data, the true solution can be pinpointed by data alone. However, when data is scarce, noisy, or incorrectly labeled, we rely on priors and hypothesis space constraints. These three tools—data, priors, and hypotheses—can constrain the search in similar ways, leading to the principle that what can be achieved with one tool can often be achieved with another. Note that the hypothesis space imposes hard constraints, while data and priors impose soft constraints that can be violated at the cost of a penalty. As Ilya Sutskever noted, many methods are essentially "extra training data in disguise."
concepts.motivation_md: This explains why domain expertise (priors/hypotheses) is critical in small-data regimes, whereas massive datasets allow for more flexible, less biased models.
concepts.recap_md: - Increasing data volume decreases the necessity for strong priors or structural constraints.

key_passage.text: The more data you have, the less you need other modeling tools. With enough data, the true solution will be pinpointed by data alone. However, when we don't have enough data, or when the data is noisy or incorrectly labeled, we can turn to our two other tools, which we will see next.

motivation.text: If you don't have much data, you can use strong priors and structural constraints instead. If you don't have much domain knowledge, you can collect lots of data instead.

concepts.title: Overfitting
concepts.one_liner: Overfitting occurs when a model fits properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data, resulting in poor generalization.
concepts.content: Overfitting happens when we fit to properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data. When this happens, training performance will be high, but test performance can be very low, since what we learned about the training data does not generalize to the test data. Learning theory studies the settings under which optimization on the training set yields good results on the test set.
concepts.motivation_md: The goal of machine learning is to perform well on new data, not just memorize the training set; understanding overfitting is crucial for building robust models.
concepts.recap_md: - It is characterized by high training performance but low test performance. - It occurs when a model captures noise or specific artifacts of the training set. - Generalization is the ability of the model to perform well on data it has not seen before.

key_passage.text: When we fit to properties in the training data that do not exist in the test data, we call this overfitting. When this happens, training performance will be high, but test performance can be very low, since what we learned about the training data does not generalize to the test data.

motivation.text: Learning theory studies the settings under which optimization on the training set yields good results on the test set. In general it may not, since the test set may have different properties from the training set.

prereq.rationale: Generalization error is defined as the expected cost incurred when sampling from the true data generating process.
The text discusses capacity specifically in the context of its tendency to lead to overfitting when too high.
Regularization is introduced as a factor that decouples the number of parameters from the actual capacity of the model.
Regularization is defined as a mechanism specifically used to prevent learning functions that are too flexible and overfit the data.
This concept builds on the idea that hypotheses are assigned prior probability mass which must be distributed across the hypothesis space.
The definition of priors as soft constraints in the search framework relies on the earlier established link between regularization and probabilistic priors.
The trade-off principle is built specifically upon the interaction between the three tools (data, priors, and hypotheses) defined in the search framework.

overlay.rationale: Underfitting and overfitting are the two primary, distinct reasons why a learner may perform poorly on test data.
Approximation error measures fit on training data, while generalization error measures fit against the ground truth relationship.
Regularization provides a mathematical way to implement the philosophical principle of Occam's razor in learning algorithms.
Lp regularization is a specific, common method of implementing the general regularization penalty R(theta).
Lp regularizers concretely demonstrate Occam's razor by forcing parameters to zero, resulting in simpler model forms.
Bayesian probability provides the formal theoretical justification for the additive structure of regularized objectives.
The Bayesian Occam's razor provides a probabilistic explanation for why simpler hypotheses are naturally preferred.
